passage:
Subject: okay so there's this girl
Hemant,
Don't laugh. There's a girl in my Economics section, Tanushree. On the first day, when Prof. Bose's mic died, she stood up and did his voice so perfectly the whole class cracked up, and even he laughed. She talks in class like she has never once worried about being wrong.
We've spoken maybe four times. Once about the canteen samosas, once about a quiz, twice in the library queue. That's it.
And yet. I've already imagined us at the college fest, then road-tripping to Goa after finals, then her meeting Amma, who would definitely love her. I've decided her favourite colour is green because of her bag.
Okay, typing it out, I can see I've built a whole person from four chats. But I swear she's brilliant.
Reply soon and tell me I'm not mad.
Raghav

qa.q: How many times has Raghav spoken to Tanushree?
qa.a: They've spoken maybe four times.

qa.q: What does Raghav's imagined road trip and Amma meeting suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: Raghav is dazzled and excited, imagining a whole future with Tanushree from four short chats.

qa.q: What could Raghav do to see the real Tanushree rather than the imagined one?
qa.a: Raghav could spend more ordinary time talking with her, in class or in a group, and let her show who she is before planning any future.

qa.q: How might Tanushree see these same four conversations?
qa.a: Tanushree may see them as friendly chats with a classmate, with no idea Raghav has already pictured road trips and family meetings.

grounding: Shows a student drawn to a classmate's humour and confidence who imagines a future from a few conversations, filling in the blanks.

Neelam, stop smiling, I'm serious. You know Mihir from design studio? The one who presented the bus-stop project and made the jury laugh three times? He walks up to the pin-up wall like it's his own living room. I've never been that sure of anything in my life.
We talked after studio on Monday for about ten minutes. About fonts! And he said my sketches "have a pulse", and I've been replaying it since.
I've decided he probably reads a lot. And he's definitely kind to his mother. And he'd be the kind of person who remembers your chai order.
What? Okay, I don't actually know any of that. I know he's funny, I know he's confident and I know he likes fonts. The rest I might have, um, invented. 😅
But it's a nice invention, na? Gargi is allowed one nice invention.

Coach's note, Thursday evening badminton practice.
Ujjwal (second year) was off his game today. Between every set he went to his bag and checked his phone, then came back either grinning or flat. Kishore, his doubles partner, told me quietly that Ujjwal had asked a girl from his class, Pallavi, for coffee on Sunday after replying to her stories for two weeks, and she hadn't answered yet.
At the water break I heard Ujjwal say, "She replied in two minutes last time. Now it's been four hours. That means no, right?" He laughed as if joking, but he served into the net three times after that.
I told him to leave the phone in the bag till practice ended, and that four hours can simply mean someone is stuck in a lab. He nodded but didn't look convinced. I'll keep his drills light this week.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal ask Pallavi?
qa.a: Ujjwal asked Pallavi for coffee on Sunday.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal afraid of as he checked his phone?
qa.a: Ujjwal was afraid Pallavi's slow reply meant rejection; the four-hour gap felt huge even though he laughed it off.

qa.q: How did the coach help at this stage, and what else might help Ujjwal?
qa.a: The coach suggested leaving the phone in the bag and pointed out other reasons for a slow reply; Ujjwal could also remind himself that one reply time is not an answer.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel watching Ujjwal this evening?
qa.a: Kishore probably feels a mix of sympathy and worry, sharing it quietly with the coach and seeing it affect their doubles game.

grounding: Shows a young man who has replied to a girl's stories and asked her for coffee, fearing rejection and treating reply speed as hugely important.

Tuesday, 1 a.m.
Replied to Riddhima's story about her rooftop plants with a sunflower. A sunflower? What was I thinking. She reacted with a laugh though. That's good? Or polite?
Finally asked if she wants to get coffee after the Friday lab. Typed it eleven times. Chinmay said "bro, just send it", grabbed my phone and pressed send before I could delete it again.
She replied: "sure, sounds fun!"
I've read that maybe forty times. "Sure" feels a bit flat. But then there's "sounds fun" with an exclamation mark. Does the exclamation mark cancel the "sure"? Chinmay says a grown man shouldn't analyse punctuation like it's a board exam.
He's right. I'm scared she's just being nice. But she said yes. She said YES.
Thomas

qa.q: How many times did Thomas type the coffee message?
qa.a: Thomas typed it eleven times.

qa.q: What is Thomas worried about when he rereads 'sure, sounds fun!'?
qa.a: Thomas is scared Riddhima is just being nice, so even the punctuation feels like a clue to whether she really wants to go.

qa.q: What could help Thomas before Friday's coffee?
qa.a: Thomas could take the yes at face value, stop decoding punctuation, and focus on enjoying an ordinary conversation with Riddhima. 😊

qa.q: How does Chinmay see Thomas's worry?
qa.a: Chinmay finds it a bit much, which is why he pressed send and joked about the board exam, but he is also nudging Thomas to be brave.

grounding: Illustrates a young man replying to a girl's stories, asking her for coffee and rereading her text, with fear of rejection under the play.

I'm Shalini, and three months into seeing Arvind, I noticed the glow had changed. It didn't vanish; it got quieter, like a song you know by heart.
I started seeing other things. He is late for everything and calls it "flexible". He goes silent for a whole evening when he's stressed, then acts as if nothing happened. And when my cousin chose a lower-paying job teaching in a village school, he called it "wasting a degree", and something in me went still.
He is also the one who stayed up till two helping me fix my thesis charts. Both are true.
My roommate Kavitha asked, "So, do you still get butterflies?"
I said, "Sometimes." Then I heard myself say what I was really thinking: "I care less about the butterflies now. I'm trying to work out if I actually like who he is."

qa.a: Arvind called it 'wasting a degree'.

Student counselling note. Sarita, 20, second year. Came in at the suggestion of her roommate, Himani.
Sarita said nothing is "wrong" with Nitin, whom she has been seeing for four months. But she is noticing things she didn't at first: he keeps money very tight and gets irritated when she spends on friends; he is warm with her but short with waiters; he wants to settle near his parents, while she has always planned to study abroad.
"At first it just felt amazing to be with him," she said. "Now I'm asking whether I actually like the person, not just the feeling." She seemed relieved, and a little sad, saying it.
We talked about how this shift is normal and useful, and that she can raise differences with Nitin directly. She plans to ask him about the study-abroad plan this weekend. Follow-up in two weeks.

qa.a: Nitin wants to settle near his parents.

qa.q: How did Sarita seem to feel as she described the shift?
qa.a: Sarita seemed relieved and a little sad: relieved to say it aloud, sad that the early glow is fading.

qa.q: What step did Sarita plan, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Sarita planned to ask Nitin about the study-abroad plan this weekend; talking directly about differences shows who he is, not just how the relationship feels.

qa.a: Himani probably noticed Sarita seemed unsettled about the relationship and wanted her to have someone neutral to think it through with.

For six weeks after we started meeting, I didn't know what Lavanya and I were. We'd go to the old bookshop on Saturdays and text every night, and then she'd mention a "coffee with someone from the gym" and I'd spend the evening guessing.
Manoj finally said, "Dhruv, you're writing thesis-length theories. Just ask her."
So last Sunday, walking back from the bookshop, I said it, badly rehearsed: "I'd like us to be only seeing each other. Where are you on that?" My ears were burning.
She stopped walking. "I was hoping you'd ask," she said. "The gym person is my cousin's friend. I wasn't sure what you wanted either."
Even now I think: if she'd said no, it would have hurt, but at least I'd have stopped guessing. Asking was the scariest ten seconds of the year. And the most useful.

qa.q: Where were Dhruv and Lavanya walking back from when Dhruv asked?
qa.a: They were walking back from the bookshop.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel while asking, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Dhruv was nervous; the words came out badly rehearsed and Dhruv's ears were burning. 😅

qa.q: Why was asking directly better than more guessing?
qa.a: Asking risked a no, but it ended six weeks of theories and gave both of them facts to act on; it also showed Lavanya had been unsure too.

qa.q: What had Lavanya been feeling during those six weeks?
qa.a: Lavanya was also unsure what Dhruv wanted and was hoping Dhruv would ask.

grounding: Shows a young adult asking directly to be exclusive, risking a no to end weeks of guessing.

passage:
Counselling note. Final-year student Rashmi, sessions 3 and 4.
Session 3: Rashmi said she and Jeevan have been meeting for two months, but she doesn't know if they are "a thing". She checks whether he posts photos with other people and loses sleep over his vague replies. We discussed that the uncertainty is costing her more than an answer would. She wrote her own sentence and practised it twice: "I like you and I'd like us to be exclusive. What do you want?"
Session 4, a week later: Rashmi said she asked him on the walk back from the metro. Jeevan said he wasn't ready for anything exclusive yet. She cried that night, she told me, but by the next day felt "weirdly lighter". "At least I'm not reading tea leaves any more." She has decided to step back from seeing him. She seemed sad but steady.

qa.q: What did Jeevan say when Rashmi asked?
qa.a: Jeevan said he wasn't ready for anything exclusive yet.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi feel 'weirdly lighter' after hearing no?
qa.a: The answer hurt, but it ended the guessing; Rashmi no longer had to read every vague reply for meaning.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help Rashmi prepare?
qa.a: The counsellor helped Rashmi see the cost of uncertainty and let her write and practise her own clear sentence, so she could ask directly.

qa.q: What might the question have been like from Jeevan's side?
qa.a: Jeevan may have felt awkward, but a clear question made it easier to give a clear answer instead of more vague replies.

passage:
You want to know if my friends ever had it hard? Listen to your Vidya Nani. This was 1998, in Hyderabad. My friend Raghav fell for Shaheen from our college, and I watched the whole thing.
First it was small things. Raghav learning to eat haleem without making a face. Shaheen learning our gang's silly nicknames. Her friends teasing him about cricket; ours teasing her about her poetry.
Then, only four months in, his mother asked the question: "And what will the children be?" Her abba asked where they would live, and whose festivals they would keep.
What I remember is this: Raghav didn't hide behind Shaheen, and she didn't hide behind him. They went to both houses together. They said, "We don't know every answer yet, but we'll decide as a pair." Not everyone was happy. But I knew then they could stand together outside, not just in the canteen.

qa.q: What did Raghav's mother ask?
qa.a: His mother asked, 'And what will the children be?'

qa.q: What did Vidya believe about the couple after they visited both houses together?
qa.a: Vidya felt confident that Raghav and Shaheen could face the outside world together, since neither hid behind the other.

qa.q: What did Raghav and Shaheen do well when the family questions came?
qa.a: They went to both houses together and answered as a pair, admitting they didn't know every answer but would decide jointly.

qa.q: How might Shaheen's abba have felt asking where they'd live?
qa.a: Her abba was probably worried about her future and traditions, and asking was his way of checking whether the couple had thought it through.

grounding: Shows a friend watching a young couple adjust to each other's food and friends and face early family questions about religion and household together.

The power went at noon on Eid, just as Rehana's family sat down to lunch in their Kozhikode flat, and the fans slowed to nothing. Jyoti, there as Rehana's college friend, watched Faraz from Lucknow sweat through his new kurta and still reach for a second helping of pathiri.
"He's learning," Rehana whispered. Two months ago he'd called Malabar biryani "too mild".
Rehana's aunt fanned herself with a plate. "So Faraz, after marriage you'll take her to Lucknow? Joint family?"
The room went quiet except for the traffic outside.
Faraz glanced at Rehana. She gave a small nod. "We've talked about it, Khala," he said. "We'd like to start on our own, near both our jobs, and visit both families often. We're still working out the details together."
The aunt raised an eyebrow. Rehana squeezed his hand under the table. Jyoti thought: they rehearsed this, and they did it side by side.

passage:
People think we decided on some romantic night. We didn't. We decided in the worst week of Gurpreet's life.
His father's shop flooded in the rains, and Gurpreet spent five days hauling wet stock and arguing on the phone. He was short-tempered and exhausted, and once he snapped at me over nothing. An hour later he came back and said, "That was unfair. I'm sorry. I'm scared." That mattered to me more than any gift.
He'd seen me at my worst too, the semester I failed stats and cried at his cousin's wedding.
So one night on the hostel steps, we talked properly. I want to do a master's in Delhi; he wants to take over the shop in Amritsar. We didn't pretend that away. We made a plan for two years apart and a date to review it.
Then I said, "I choose this. With my eyes open." And he said, "Me too." That's Madhuri's great romance.

qa.q: What happened to Gurpreet's father's shop?
qa.a: His father's shop flooded in the rains.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet's apology matter so much to Madhuri?
qa.a: It showed that under stress Gurpreet could own his mistakes and be honest about fear, which told Madhuri more than any gift.

qa.q: What makes this commitment grounded rather than just a feeling?
qa.a: They had seen each other in hard times, talked openly about clashing goals, and made a plan with a review date before choosing each other.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt hearing 'I choose this. With my eyes open'?
qa.a: Gurpreet likely felt trusted and steady, knowing Madhuri chose him after seeing his worst week, not just his good days.

grounding: Shows a couple committing after seeing each other under stress and speaking honestly about goals, as a clear-eyed decision.

I've been Mehak's roommate for three years, so I've seen her with Irfan through most of it. The first months were all giggles on the phone and roses on Valentine's Day. Cute, but I didn't think much of it.
What changed my mind was last winter. Mehak's mother was in hospital for weeks, and Irfan sat in that hospital corridor every evening after his internship, with food, and just listened. When he lost his placement offer in March, Mehak didn't give him a speech. She helped him redo his CV at 2 a.m.
Last month I heard them on our balcony talking about jobs, cities, money, even how many years before marriage. Serious, calm voices. No roses.
Then Mehak came in and said, "We've decided. We're committed." She didn't look dreamy. She looked certain. I can't know everything they feel, but to me, Sonali, it looked like a choice they'd made together.

qa.a: Irfan sat in that hospital corridor every evening after his internship.

qa.q: What does Mehak's certain, not dreamy, look suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Mehak made a clear-eyed decision, not a swept-away feeling, after seeing Irfan in hard times.

qa.q: What helped this couple reach a grounded commitment?
qa.a: They supported each other through real stress, like the hospital weeks and the lost placement, and then talked honestly about jobs, cities and money.

qa.q: How has Sonali's view of the couple changed over three years?
qa.a: Sonali first saw giggles and roses and didn't think much of it; after watching them through hard times, Sonali saw a real choice made together.

Sunaina's mother had set it up through a family friend, so Sunaina went to the café in Koregaon Park expecting to be polite for an hour and leave.
Vikas turned out to be funny. He did a wicked impression of his manager and admitted he'd spent the whole morning choosing a shirt. She laughed more than she'd planned.
But under the laughter, a list kept running. He'd mentioned a possible transfer to Singapore next year. She had just been made team lead in Pune and loved it. He talked about "settling down soon"; she wanted two more years before thinking about marriage at all.
When the bill came, he asked, "Can I see you again?" She felt a real flutter, and at the same moment a small, practical voice asking, And then what?
"Yes," she said. "But I have questions. Real ones."
"Good," Vikas said. "So do I."

qa.a: Vikas mentioned a possible transfer to Singapore next year.

By their third month, Francis and Ankita had a rhythm. A good-morning text before his local train, a photo of her lunch at one, a voice note at night when she was too tired to type. Saturdays were for the vegetable market in Bandra and whatever film was showing.
On Thursday Ankita had a client presentation she'd been dreading all week. At seven that morning her phone buzzed: "Slide 12. You've got this. Breathe before the numbers." He had remembered the slide number from a rant she'd made on Monday.
She didn't cry, exactly, but she had to stand still by the kettle for a moment.
Later she told her sister, "He didn't send flowers. He remembered slide twelve."
Her sister laughed. Ankita didn't. That was when she realised she had started to count on him.

qa.q: What did Francis's message on Thursday morning say?
qa.a: It said, 'Slide 12. You've got this. Breathe before the numbers.'

qa.q: Why did Ankita have to stand still by the kettle?
qa.a: Ankita was moved that Francis had remembered the exact slide from Monday's rant; it made her feel truly listened to.

qa.a: Small, dependable acts like remembering a deadline build trust more than grand gestures, so both can keep noticing these details.

qa.a: Her sister laughed, perhaps expecting something more romantic, and may not yet see how much that small act meant to Ankita.

passage:
Sunday night
First real fight with Adil. Not a sulky one, a real one.
It was about his parents. He'd told them we'd come for lunch every Sunday "from now on", without asking me. I said I also need Sundays for my own family and, honestly, for sleep. He said, "But that's how it's always been in our house." I said, "It's not only your house any more."
He went quiet and walked to the window. I thought, here we go, the silent treatment. But after a few minutes he came back and said, "You're right that I should have asked. I'm upset, but I'm not going anywhere. Can we work out a schedule?"
I'd braced for him to storm off. Instead he stayed in the room while being angry. Nandini always says the first fight tells you more than the first date. I think she's right.
Farida

qa.a: Adil had told them they'd come for lunch every Sunday 'from now on'.

passage:
When Mehak first said, "What if we just got one flat instead of two?", I said, "Yes, obviously," and meant it. Then over the next month I got quieter and quieter.
I love her. I love waking up to her humming and the way she argues with the TV news. But every time she sent me a listing, something in my chest tightened, like a door slowly swinging shut. No more evenings alone with my music loud. No more coming home to just me.
I didn't say anything, which I now know was the problem. Mehak thought I was losing interest. One night she asked, "Do you not want this?" and I finally said it: "I do. And I'm scared. Both."
